hints: Remember that addition polymerisation simply opens the C=C double bond into a C-C single bond, so work backwards from single to double.
Split the four-carbon backbone into two two-carbon monomer units, the first is $-CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-$ and the second is $-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-$.
Put the C=C double bond back between the two carbons of each unit and add back the H atoms to see the original alkenes.
walkthrough:
**Recall how addition polymers form**

Think of polymerisation as unzipping a C=C double bond to make two new single bonds. To find the monomer, we do the reverse and zip it back up.

Rule to reverse:
$$-CH_2-CH_2- \text{ (polymer)} \rightarrow CH_2=CH_2 \text{ (monomer)}$$

**Split the section into two monomers**

This is a co-polymer from two different alkenes, so cut the 4-carbon chain in the middle. That gives two 2-carbon fragments.

$$-CH_2-C(CH_3)_2- \text{ + } -CH(CH_3)-CH_2-$$

**Reform the double bonds**

Now place a double bond between the two carbons in each fragment. The first fragment becomes $CH_2=C(CH_3)_2$, which is methylpropene (2-methylpropene). The second fragment becomes $CH_2=CH(CH_3)$, which is propene. This matches the pair of monomers.

options.A: But-1-ene is $CH_2=CHCH_2CH_3$ and would polymerise to $-CH_2-CH(CH_2CH_3)-$. This gives an ethyl side chain, not the $-C(CH_3)_2-$ unit with two methyl branches seen in the section.
options.B: But-2-ene is $CH_3CH=CHCH_3$ and would polymerise to $-CH(CH_3)-CH(CH_3)-$. This would give two adjacent CH groups each with one methyl, not a $CH_2$ next to a $C(CH_3)_2$ group.
options.C: Ethene $CH_2=CH_2$ would give only $-CH_2-CH_2-$ with no branches. Pent-2-ene $CH_3CH=CHCH_2CH_3$ would give longer ethyl and methyl branches. Neither can produce the $C(CH_3)_2$ carbon with two methyl groups.
options.D: Methylpropene $CH_2=C(CH_3)_2$ opens to give $-CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-$, exactly the left half. Propene $CH_2=CHCH_3$ opens to give $-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-$, which is the same as $-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-$ depending on orientation, exactly the right half.
